summary: Describes how to protect passive optical network access by using more than one optical line terminal, with MPLS used at the network edge to provide the redundancy. The goal is that a customer stays connected if one terminal or path fails.

eli5.summary: A house has two doors so you can still get out if one is blocked. This lets a fiber-optic neighborhood connection use a backup entrance to the network.

questions: mpls protection for passive optical networks
how does pon trunk protection work
what is an olt in a passive optical network
subtitle: Extending ICCP so two MPLS-capable optical line terminals can back each other up and keep passive optical network customers online.

tldr.problem: Passive optical networks (PON) used as backhaul for mobile small cells and Wi-Fi hotspots serve many subscribers per port, yet traditionally had no redundancy. With trunk protection, all traffic including OAM is blocked on the protection link, so end-to-end protection mechanisms cannot work.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8024 extends the Inter-Chassis Communication Protocol (ICCP) with four PON TLVs so a working OLT and a protection OLT can exchange PON port state. Together with pseudowire preferential forwarding status, this lets traffic switch to the protection OLT and its protection pseudowire.
tldr.outcome: The RFC specifies the TLV formats, the four failure procedures and the IANA values. Synchronizing ONU configuration data is left out of scope.

today: RFC 8024 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2016, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 7275 and RFC 6870.

sections.title: Why PON Needs Multi-Chassis Protection
sections.content:
MPLS is being extended to the edge of operator networks, including the access nodes. A Passive Optical Network (PON) delivers high bandwidth (1 Gbps or even 10 Gbps) to a dozen or more subscribers at once. In the past, access technologies such as PON and DSL were used for subscribers with no redundancy. Growth in mobile data changed that: PON is considered a viable low-cost backhaul for LTE small cells and Wi-Fi hotspots, and a PON port serving a dozen of them could carry hundreds of simultaneous subscribers. Such backhaul wants the economics of PON but also the first-mile protection normally found in point-to-point access.

The RFC builds on the optical-layer Trunk protection described in IEEE 1904.1. A working OLT and its working trunk fiber are backed by a protection OLT and a protection trunk fiber behind the same optical splitter. It is cheaper than Tree protection, which duplicates the whole optical distribution network, but it protects only part of the path from the OLT to the ONUs.

With this architecture all traffic, including link OAM, is blocked on the protection link. That frustrates end-to-end mechanisms such as ITU-T G.8031, so the OLTs need a signaling channel to exchange PON link status, registered ONU information and network status.

sections.title: The Protection Architecture
sections.content:
The OLTs have MPLS functionality. The working OLT connects to a provider edge router (PE) by a working pseudowire (PW), and the protection OLT connects to the same PE (a single PE) or to a second PE (dual-homing PEs) by a protection PW. The PWs provide transport between the ONUs and a Customer Edge (CE) and can protect each other. The OLTs and PEs are assumed to work in the independent mode of PW redundancy from RFC 6870.

The signaling channel is ICCP, the Inter-Chassis Communication Protocol of RFC 7275. ICCP synchronizes state and configuration between two or more PEs and so far defined application messages only for Pseudowire Redundancy and Multi-Chassis LACP. The RFC proposes treating PON as another case of attachment circuit redundancy, and extends ICCP for it.
sections.eli5: Two doorways lead to the same building. Each doorway has its own hallway, and a manager at the far end picks whichever one is open.

sections.title: The Four PON TLVs
sections.content:
RFC 8024 defines four Type-Length-Value (TLV) objects for ICCP. In all of them the U and F bits are 0.

  • PON Connect TLV (0x200D) travels in the RG Connect message to establish the PON application connection. It carries a Protocol Version, set to 0x0001, and an Acknowledgement bit A that MUST be 1 if the sender has already received a PON Connect TLV from the recipient. No optional Sub-TLVs are defined.
  • PON Disconnect TLV (0x200E) travels in the RG Disconnect message to say the PON application connection is ending.
  • PON Configuration TLV (0x200F) travels in the RG Application Data message and announces an OLT's parameters to the other members of its Redundancy Group (RG). It holds an 8-octet System ID (the chassis MAC address), a 2-octet System Priority and a 2-octet PON Port ID. The OLT with the numerically lower System Priority has the higher priority.
  • PON State TLV (0x2010) also travels in RG Application Data and reports PON state. It holds the Redundant Object ID (ROID) from RFC 7275, a Local PON Port State and a Remote PON Port State. For each state the last bit is a fault indication for the PON port associated with the PW (1 for in fault, 0 for normal).

sections.title: Protection Procedures
sections.content:
The RFC describes four failure cases.

PON link failure. The working OLT turns off its faulty PON interface so the protection trunk link can be activated. It MUST send an LDP fault notification with the status bit Local AC (ingress) Receive Fault set to its peer PE, and MUST send an ICCP message with a PON State TLV with Local PON Port State set to the protection OLT. On receiving that, the protection OLT MUST activate the protection PON link and advertise the protection PW with the Preferential Forwarding status bit of active to the remote PE. Following RFC 6870, the remote PE matches local and remote status and selects PW2 as the new active PW.

PW failure. This procedure is for link-sparse access or aggregation networks where LSP-layer protection is impossible. When a fault is detected on the working PW (for example by VCCV BFD), the working OLT SHOULD turn off its PON interface and send the same PON State TLV. The protection OLT MUST activate its interface to the protection trunk fiber and MUST send the Preferential Forwarding active notification to the remote PE.

Working OLT failure. With a single PE, if PE1 loses its connection to the working OLT it SHOULD send an LDP notification on the protection PW with the Request Switchover bit set. The protection OLT MUST then activate its optical interface to the protection trunk fiber and the protection PW.

Dual-homing PE. The PW-RED State TLV of RFC 7275 can be used by PE1 to notify PE2 of faults in all of these scenarios, and PE2 then acts as described above.

sections.title: ONU Database Synchronization
sections.content:
If the working and protection OLTs do not share information about registered ONUs, all registered ONUs would be de-registered and have to re-register during a switchover, which would significantly increase protection time. For fast switchover, both OLTs need to know the protected ONUs, and the operational state and significant configuration of each ONU and its provisioned services must be distributed to both.

How to synchronize that data (examples given are ONU MAC address, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and VLAN identifiers) is outside the scope of this document. It may be done by a policy mechanism, provisioned in the management plane, or done by other signaling.
sections.eli5: The spare door only helps if its guard already knows who lives inside. Otherwise everyone has to check in again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Like ICCP itself, this application SHOULD only be used in well-managed and highly monitored service provider PON access networks in a single administrative domain. That includes rogue ONU attachment detection and mitigation through device authentication. Many security considerations of RFC 7275 apply.

Optical paths between the OLT and ONUs often cross publicly accessible facilities such as telephone poles, so optical impairment can cause excessive link bouncing. ICCP runs in the MPLS domain and does not cross the PON, but a malicious ONU could still cause link bouncing and so increase ICCP exchanges. Operators should restrict unauthorized ONUs and limit the impact of link bouncing at the OLT.
sections.eli5: Only trusted guards should use the walkie-talkie, and nobody should be able to plug in a fake door that keeps flickering open and shut.
